parts.title: My life as a school reporter
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last year, I became the editor of our school newspaper. I was only fourteen, and I did not know much about journalism, but I loved writing and I wanted to learn.

Our team has ten members, and we meet every Wednesday to decide the stories for the next issue. Some people write about sport, others about music or school trips. My favourite job is the interview. Last month, I talked to our head teacher about the new rules for mobile phones, and I was very nervous. She answered all my questions, and she even laughed at one of my jokes.

The hardest part of the work is the deadline. Every article must be ready by Friday at noon, and sometimes, we have to stay late to finish. Once, a page was empty on Thursday night, and we wrote a story about the school cat in just twenty minutes!

The best moment came when a local newspaper printed one of our stories about the town library. I felt so proud. Now I think I would like to become a real journalist, but my mother says that I should become a doctor first.

options: She refused to answer some questions

questions.explanation: She answered all the questions and laughed at a joke.

parts.title: The history of the newspaper
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
The first printed newspapers appeared in Europe about four hundred years ago. [1] They were small, with only a few pages, and they were published once a week.

At that time, most people could not read. [2] Someone would read the news aloud in a café or a market, and everybody gathered around to listen.

In the nineteenth century, new machines made printing much faster. [3] A newspaper could now be sold for a penny, so even poor families could buy one.

The invention of the telegraph helped too. [4] News from other countries could arrive in a few hours instead of several weeks.

Today, many people read the news on their phones. [5] Some newspapers have even stopped printing on paper altogether.
sentences: Messages could now travel along wires between cities.
Because of this, reading aloud was an important way to share information.
Some newspapers are free, and people read them on the train.
The best reporters were paid large sums of money by the kings.
This has changed the business of journalism enormously.
As a result, newspapers became much cheaper.
Nobody had ever seen anything like them before.
That was why the news was always a few days old.

gaps.explanation: Nobody had seen anything like them before leads to the description of them being small.
Because people could not read, reading aloud was important, and the next sentence shows someone reading in a café.
Faster printing made newspapers cheaper, which explains why the next sentence says a newspaper could be sold for a penny.
The telegraph sent messages along wires, and the next sentence says news from other countries arrived in a few hours.
The change to phones has changed journalism, and some papers stopped printing on paper.

parts.title: How to spot fake news
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: These days, we see news all the time, [1] not everything that we read is true. Some websites write stories that are completely false, [2] they want people to click on them and spend time on their pages. Before you share a story with your friends, you [3] to ask a few questions. Who wrote it? Is the same story on other websites? Does the photo look real? If a story seems too amazing to be true, it is often [4] true. You should also be careful with stories [5] make you very angry or afraid. A good rule is to wait before sharing. If in doubt, check with a teacher or look at [6] trusted website.

gaps.explanation: We see news all the time, but not everything is true: contrast.
They write false stories because they want people to click.
"You need to ask a few questions" gives advice before you share a story.
A story that seems too amazing is often not true.
Stories that make you angry: a relative pronoun for things.
Look at a trusted website: indefinite article before an adjective.

parts.title: Short conversations

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Good evening, and welcome to Channel Nine. A change in tonight’s schedule. The football match went into extra time, so all the programmes are late. Our newspaper guide says that the main news starts at seven, but please forget that, because it was the old timetable. Before the news, we will show the match highlights and a short weather report. Normally we start at a quarter past six, as you know, but not today. The main news will begin at half past seven, with all the day’s stories and an interview with the mayor. Thank you for your patience.

question.prompt: When will the main news begin tonight?
question.explanation: The guide says seven but that was the old timetable, and the normal start is a quarter past six; tonight it is half past seven.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Morning! Are you after the newspaper?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Yes. Is it free to read in here? I saw a sign.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It used to be free for everybody who sat in the cafe, but we stopped that in the summer, because too many people stayed all day. Now it costs a pound if you just read it.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Oh, that’s a pity. Do you have any offers?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Next month we’ll have one for people who bring a friend, two papers for the price of one. But today, if you order a coffee, you can read the paper for nothing.

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: m

turns.speaker: m

parts.title: A talk about a radio station
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: mariam
turns.text: Good morning, everybody, and welcome to our radio station. My name is Dinah, and I am the manager. We went on the air twenty years ago, although the idea started in 1998, a few years before. At first we had only two presenters and a tiny studio, in what is now the kitchen. Today we have more than two hundred thousand listeners. I know that sounds small beside the big national stations, which have millions, but for a local station it’s a lot, and the number grows every year. People often ask me when we are busiest. You would think that it’s the evening, when people are at home, but the busiest time is the morning, between seven and nine, when people are driving to work and listening to the traffic news and the music. Weekends are different. On Saturdays we play a lot of music from the charts, but on Sundays we invite local bands to play live in the studio. Last year we had a choir as well, but the bands are what people love. Now, who makes all this happen? We have five paid staff, and about thirty volunteers. A few years ago there were only fifteen, but more people join each month. Some are students, some are retired, and all of them love the radio. Finally, please come to our open day. Many of you ask whether it is on a Sunday, because on that day we are usually closed to visitors, but this time it will be on Saturday, the second of June. Come and see the studio, meet the presenters, and try reading the news yourselves. Entry is free, and there will be tea and cakes. Thank you for coming this morning, and I hope to see you again soon.

gaps.explanation: The idea started a few years before, but it went on the air twenty years ago.
Big national stations have millions, but this station has more than two hundred thousand listeners.

gaps.prompt: Most people listen to the radio in the
gaps.explanation: You might guess the evening, but the busiest time is the morning.

gaps.prompt: Live music in the studio on Sundays comes from local
gaps.explanation: The choir was last year; on Sundays local bands play live.

gaps.prompt: The station relies on about ___ unpaid helpers
gaps.explanation: There were only fifteen a few years ago, but now there are about thirty volunteers.

gaps.prompt: Visitors are welcome at the open day on
gaps.explanation: The studio is usually closed on Sundays, but the open day is on Saturday.

parts.title: An interview with a news photographer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Dorrit, you’ve been a news photographer for fifteen years. How did you earn your first money from photography?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: It was a long time ago. I took a photo of a fire near my school when I was sixteen. I’d entered a school contest before, but I didn’t win anything, just a certificate. And I did sell my old camera once, to buy a better one, but that was money for equipment, not for pictures. A local paper saw my fire photo and paid me fifty pounds for it. I was so proud.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you like most about your job now?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Honestly, the surprises. People think it’s about a fixed plan, but there is no routine. I never know what the day will bring. I get a call in the morning and I could be at a football stadium, or in a hospital by the afternoon. And I’m often alone, so I don’t have the same team around me every day. I wouldn’t change that. I’d be bored with a regular programme.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the most difficult part of the work?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Waiting, definitely. You can stand in the rain for six hours and the important moment lasts two seconds. Writing captions is annoying, because the editor wants every name correct, but it’s easy compared to waiting. And travel? I used to dread flights, but I’m used to them now.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: You were once caught in a storm. What changed after that?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Oh, that was frightening. I was on a beach, taking photos, when the wind suddenly became very strong. My camera was fine, luckily, so I didn’t buy a new one. I didn’t want to stop covering events either, that is my life. But now I always check the weather forecast before I go out. I never did that before.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: There’s a famous photo of yours of a boy. Why does it mean so much to you?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: He was seven and he was sitting in front of his house after a flood. The photo did win a prize, but that isn’t the reason. It was also on the front of a magazine for a week, which was nice. What matters is that after people saw it, readers sent money and a company gave the family a new home. That makes me proud.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to young photographers?

turns.speaker: p
turns.text: Don’t think you need the best equipment, my first good photos were taken with a cheap camera. And don’t think that you must work only for the big newspapers, small local ones are a great start. But what I would say above all is to be kind to the people you photograph. They’re often having the worst day of their lives.

Do you like writing? What do you write?
Have you ever been in a photograph in the newspaper?
What do you do at the weekend?

parts.title: Describe a photograph
parts.instructions: Look at the photograph and speak for about one minute. Describe what you can see and say what the people might be feeling.
parts.prompt: A reporter interviewing a man in a uniform on a street.

parts.title: Talk about the topic
parts.instructions: Answer the questions. Try to give a reason or an example with each answer.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to know what is happening in the world?
Do you think that children should read the news? Why or why not?
What makes a news story interesting?
